methods.notes: WLED registers two mDNS services on port 80 — "_wled._tcp" and "_http._tcp" — and adds a single TXT record, mac. Browse the WLED service type rather than _http._tcp: the latter matches every web server on the LAN, including printers and routers.

Fallback only, for firmware or forks that do not register the WLED service type. Anything found this way must be confirmed by fetching /json/info and checking info.brand before it is offered as a WLED device.

discovery.notes: info.mac from /json/info is the identity key that survives a rename, a DHCP lease change and a firmware update. Do not key on IP: these are DHCP clients on consumer routers. Do not key on the user-set name either — WLED installs commonly run several controllers whose owner has named them by room, and names get reused.

identification.hostname_notes: Default mDNS name is "wled-" plus the last six hex characters of the MAC, set in wled00/wled.cpp when the configured name is still the compile-time default. Users can and do change it, so it is a hint for display, never an identity key.

device.name: WLED Addressable LED Controller
device.notes:
WLED is open-source firmware for addressable LED strips on ESP8266 and ESP32 boards. It is not a product with a manufacturer — the same firmware runs on bare dev boards, on purpose-built controllers (QuinLED, Athom, Dig-Uno/Dig-Quad) and on retail strips reflashed by their owners, so the device this spec describes is the firmware and its network surface, not a SKU.
Two distinct interface families live here and are easy to confuse. The control plane — JSON over HTTP, a WebSocket, the legacy /win API and optionally MQTT — is how a client sets brightness, effects, segments and presets, and is what an app such as WLED+ speaks. The realtime plane — E1.31/sACN, Art-Net, DDP, TPM2.net and WLED's own WARLS family — streams per-pixel data and bypasses the effect engine entirely. A controller receiving realtime data ignores its own effects until the stream stops and the timeout expires, so a client that mixes the two planes without accounting for that will appear to have its commands ignored.

openness.notes:
This entry is the exception in this registry, and it is here to make the exception visible rather than to pad the count. Nothing below was recovered: WLED publishes its protocol, ships the firmware under a free licence, and treats third-party clients as the point rather than as a threat. What this file does is normalise that published protocol into the registry's shape so a consumer can enumerate it the same way it enumerates everything else, and so we have a worked example of what the other sixty-odd specs are trying to reconstruct.
Follow the citations before this file. Every fact here came from upstream documentation or from reading WLED's own source; no WLED hardware was in the loop, which is why nothing below claims `confirmed`. Where a port or a default is quoted, it was read out of the named source file rather than remembered — `wled00/const.h` for the access-point defaults and the realtime-mode enum, `wled00/src/dependencies/e131/ESPAsyncE131.h` for the E1.31/Art-Net/DDP ports, `wled00/wled.cpp` for the mDNS registration.
The corollary matters for anyone planning work against it: an open protocol is a moving one. WLED can and does change its JSON surface between releases, and upstream is entitled to. Pin behaviour to the `info.ver`/`info.vid` a device reports rather than to this document.

credentials.notes: WLED issues no per-client credential: anything that can reach port 80 has full control, including the settings pages, unless OTA lock is enabled. There is no pairing step, no token and no per-client identity to store. For a consumer this cuts both ways — nothing to manage, and no way to tell one client from another — and it means network reach is the whole of the security model. Treat a WLED controller as trusting its LAN completely.
stored_on_device: OTA lock passphrase, when OTA lock is enabled (default 'wledota')
MQTT broker credentials, when MQTT is configured

factory_reset.effect: The Security-page reset deletes all custom settings data — passwords, configuration, macros and presets. The >12s button hold erases flash, which additionally clears WiFi credentials and returns the board to first-boot AP mode. The >6s hold is the narrower one worth knowing: it resets only the WiFi settings, leaving presets and effects intact. (The docs' >6s/>12s carry margin over the code thresholds, which are 5000 ms and 10000 ms in wled00/button.cpp — holding past the documented figures satisfies both.)

procedures.name: Hold button 0 for more than 6 seconds (WiFi settings only)

steps.action: Hold the button on GPIO 0 for more than 6 seconds and release.
steps.expect: WiFi settings return to defaults; the setup AP comes back.

procedures.indicator: Controller reboots into first-boot state with no presets.
procedures.name: Hold button 0 for more than 12 seconds (erase flash)

steps.action: Hold the button on GPIO 0 for more than 12 seconds and release.
steps.expect: Flash erased; the device behaves as freshly flashed.
steps.notes: Presets and segment layout are lost. Export them from /presets.json first — on a large install that configuration is hours of work and there is no undo.

procedures.name: Factory reset from the web UI

steps.action: Open Config → Security & Updates and use the factory reset control.
steps.expect: All custom settings data is deleted.
steps.notes: Requires the device to still be reachable, which the button holds do not. This is the path when the board is boxed into a fixture and its button is not accessible.

methods.description: The board hosts an open-to-anyone-who-reads-the-manual WPA2 access point named WLED-AP and serves its settings UI on 4.3.2.1, with an embedded DNS server answering every name so any browser navigation lands on the captive portal.

credential_encryption.notes: None. The home network passphrase is submitted as a plain HTTP form field to 4.3.2.1 over an access point whose own passphrase is a published constant. In practice the exposure window is the few seconds of the form POST within radio range, but it is a real one and a consumer automating this flow should say so rather than present provisioning as secure.

softap.passphrase_source: Compile-time default "wled1234" (DEFAULT_AP_PASS in wled00/const.h), published in WLED's own getting-started guide. Changeable in WiFi settings and worth changing, but a client should assume the documented default.

steps.action: Power the controller with no WiFi configured.
steps.expect: WLED-AP appears as an access point.

steps.action: Join WLED-AP using the documented passphrase.
Open http://4.3.2.1/ (or any URL — the captive DNS redirects), then Config → WiFi Setup.
steps.expect: WLED settings page served on port 80.

steps.action: Submit the home network SSID and passphrase, and optionally set the mDNS name.
steps.notes: Field names are those of WLED's own settings form. Treat them as a convenience for automation, not as a stable API: the settings pages are UI, and unlike the JSON API they carry no compatibility promise across releases. Driving the UI form is the documented path today; /json/cfg is the more durable one where the firmware build supports it.

arguments.description: Client SSID — the home network to join.
arguments.name: CS

arguments.description: Client passphrase, sent in the clear. Named CP up to v0.14.x; renamed PW0…PWn when multi-WiFi landed in v0.15.0 (wled00/set.cpp).
arguments.name: PW0

arguments.description: mDNS name; the device becomes reachable at <CM>.local.
arguments.name: CM

steps.action: Save; the controller reboots and joins the home network.

methods.description: Vendor-assembled controllers (Athom and similar) ship pre-flashed and may be adopted through their own onboarding before WLED's, but the WiFi step above is the same one underneath.

steps.action: Follow the assembler's quick-start, which lands on the WLED-AP portal above.

setup.notes: A factory-fresh board comes up as its own access point with a captive portal, takes the home network's credentials over plain HTTP, and reboots onto the LAN. The flow below is from WLED's own getting-started guide and settings documentation; it has not been replayed here, hence medium rather than high.

rejoin.notes: WiFi settings can be rewritten from the settings UI while the device is still on the old network, which is the ordinary router-replacement path. If the old network is already gone, the recovery AP covers it: WLED reopens WLED-AP when it cannot connect, governed by the "AP opens" setting. That behaviour can be disabled in Security settings, and a controller with the recovery AP disabled and no reachable network needs one of the button holds above.

steps.action: While still reachable, open Config → WiFi Setup and enter the new SSID and passphrase.
Save; the controller reboots onto the new network.

firmware_variants.description: The same JSON and WebSocket API is spoken by several firmware lines, which is why a client should feature-detect rather than branch on a version string. WLED+ names these as its supported set, and it is a reasonable compatibility floor for any new client.
firmware_variants.notes:
Gate on info.vid and on the presence of a field, not on parsing info.ver. Fork version strings are not ordered against mainline's and cannot be compared numerically.
Release status (verified 2026-07-31): latest release is v16.0.1 (2026-07-07); v16.0.0 "Niji" (2026-05-03) was the major one — new ESP-IDF major underneath, segment layering, particle-system effects, GIF and HUB75 matrix support, DMX input. The official WLED app is now legacy and unmaintained; upstream endorses "WLED Native" (Moustachauve) instead. ESP8266 is end-of-life — the getting-started guide advises against building new setups on it.

variants.description: Sound-reactive fork adding audio-driven effects and the sound-sync UDP channel. Extends the effect list, so effect indices are not comparable with mainline at the same version.
variants.name: WLED SR (Sound Reactive)

variants.description: Community fork with additional effects and usermods. Broadly API-compatible; WLED+ supports it on a best-effort basis.
variants.name: MoonModules

http_endpoints.description: Everything at once: state, info, effects and palettes. Convenient for a first contact, wasteful as a poll — effects and palettes are static for a given firmware build and can run to tens of kilobytes. Fetch this once on discovery, then poll /json/state or take the WebSocket.
http_endpoints.name: Full API response

fields.description: Current light state; the writable half of the API.
fields.name: state

fields.description: Read-only device metadata.
fields.name: info

fields.description: Effect names, indexed by the seg.fx value that selects them.
fields.name: effects

fields.description: Palette names, indexed by the seg.pal value that selects them.
fields.name: palettes

http_endpoints.description: The state object alone — the correct poll target.
http_endpoints.name: Read light state

fields.description: Power state.
fields.name: on

fields.description: Master brightness, 0-255. bri 0 is not the same as on:false; WLED treats them separately.
fields.name: bri

fields.description: Crossfade duration in 100ms units, 0-65535.
fields.name: transition

fields.description: Currently applied preset, -1 to 250. -1 means none.
fields.name: ps

fields.description: Currently running playlist, -1 to 250. Read-only.
fields.name: pl

fields.description: Nightlight timer settings.
fields.name: nl

fields.description: UDP sync send/receive toggles for this state change.
fields.name: udpn

fields.description: True while a realtime source is driving the LEDs.
fields.name: live

fields.description: Live data override: 0 off, 1 until the stream ends, 2 until reboot.
fields.name: lor

fields.description: Segment array. Each entry carries its own start/stop, colours (col), effect (fx), speed (sx), intensity (ix) and palette (pal). Segments are the unit almost every real control operation acts on.
fields.name: seg

http_endpoints.description: Accepts a partial state object and applies it. Send only the keys being changed — a full round-trip of a previously read state will also replay fields such as ps and can undo a preset the user just selected.
http_endpoints.name: Set light state

fields.description: true, false, or the string "t" to toggle without knowing the current state.
fields.name: on

fields.description: Master brightness.
fields.name: bri

fields.description: Crossfade for this change, in 100ms units.
fields.name: transition

fields.description: Preset to apply.
fields.name: ps

fields.description: Per-segment changes; include each segment's id to address it.
fields.name: seg

fields.description: When true, the response body is the full updated state — one round trip instead of a write followed by a read.
fields.name: v

http_endpoints.description: Accepts the same state object as /json/state; the JSON API treats them alike for writes.
http_endpoints.name: Set state (alias)

http_endpoints.description: Read-only metadata. This is the endpoint that identifies a device as WLED.
http_endpoints.name: Device information

fields.description: Human-readable firmware version, e.g. "0.15.0".
fields.name: ver

fields.description: Build ID as a date-derived integer. Compare against this, not against ver, when gating on firmware age.
fields.name: vid

fields.description: User-set friendly name. Display it; never key on it.
fields.name: name

fields.description: MAC address, hex, no separators. The stable identity key.
fields.name: mac

fields.description: Current IP address.
fields.name: ip

fields.description: Platform, e.g. "esp8266" or "esp32".
fields.name: arch

fields.description: Vendor string, normally "WLED". Use it to confirm an _http._tcp hit is really WLED.
fields.name: brand

fields.description: Product string, normally "FOSS".
fields.name: product

fields.description: UDP notifier/sync port this device is listening on. Read it rather than assuming 21324 — it is user-configurable.
fields.name: udpport

fields.description: LED configuration: count, segment capacity, power draw and the lc capability bitfield.
fields.name: leds

fields.description: Number of effects, matching the /json/eff array length.
fields.name: fxcount

fields.description: Number of palettes.
fields.name: palcount

fields.description: Seconds since boot. A drop signals a reboot, and with it any state a client cached.
fields.name: uptime

fields.description: MAC-derived unique ID, added in 16.0.0. A better stable key candidate than mac for clients.
fields.name: device_id

fields.description: PSRAM size in bytes, added in 16.0.0 (a psram_free field accompanies it).
fields.name: psram

fields.description: Source repository the build came from, added in 16.0.0.
fields.name: repo

http_endpoints.description: Effect names as an array; the index is the value written to seg.fx. Build-specific — sound-reactive forks add entries and shift nothing, but a fork may reorder.
http_endpoints.name: Effect list

http_endpoints.description: Palette names as an array; the index is the value written to seg.pal.
http_endpoints.name: Palette list

http_endpoints.description: Per-effect parameter metadata — which sliders and colour slots each effect actually uses. This is what lets a UI show the right controls per effect instead of all of them.
http_endpoints.name: Effect metadata

http_endpoints.description: Other WLED devices this one has seen on the UDP sync channel. A cheap second discovery path: find one controller and it will name its peers, which catches devices whose mDNS is being dropped by the network.
http_endpoints.name: Known WLED nodes

http_endpoints.description: Full configuration document, including WiFi, sync, MQTT and LED hardware setup. Writable by POST on builds that permit it, which makes it the durable alternative to driving the settings form. Contains credentials — treat the response as secret and never log it verbatim.
http_endpoints.name: Device configuration

http_endpoints.description: state plus info without the effect and palette arrays — the efficient poll when a client wants both.
http_endpoints.name: State and info

http_endpoints.description: All stored presets and playlists as JSON. This is the backup a user needs before any factory reset, and the whole of what is lost without one.
http_endpoints.name: Preset store

http_endpoints.description: The pre-JSON query-parameter API — /win&T=1 to turn on, &A= for brightness, &FX= for effect — answering with XML. Retained for compatibility and still the easiest thing to fire from a shell script or a button macro. New clients should use the JSON API; this one is documented because devices and integrations in the wild still speak it.
http_endpoints.name: Legacy HTTP API

http_endpoints.description: ArduinoOTA-style web upload for firmware replacement. Gated by the OTA lock passphrase when that is enabled in Security settings. Listed for completeness — the ability to replace the firmware is the freedom that makes the rest of this spec unnecessary in the first place.
http_endpoints.name: OTA firmware update

covers: Power, brightness, colour, effects, palettes, segments, presets and playlists over the JSON API
Push state updates over the WebSocket
Per-pixel realtime streaming over E1.31/sACN, Art-Net, DDP, TPM2.net and the WARLS family
MQTT against a broker the user runs
Firmware replacement over OTA or USB
local_access.notes: Optional outbound integrations exist (Alexa emulation, Hue polling, Blynk in older builds) but none is required and none carries a function that is otherwise unavailable. Nothing stops working if the device never reaches the internet.
local_access.summary: Local control is the primary interface, not a fallback. WLED has no vendor cloud, requires no account, and every function in this spec works with the controller and the client on the same LAN and nothing else.

group_topic.description: An optional second topic, shared by several controllers, carrying the same three subscribe paths ({group}, {group}/col, {group}/api). Factory default is "wled/all" (mqttGroupTopic in wled00/wled.h, unchanged v0.14.4 through v16.0.1); emptying it disables group subscription.

mqtt_configuration.notes: MQTT is off by default and points at a broker the user runs; there is no vendor broker and no account. Available since WLED 0.8.0. The long- announced breaking restructuring of the MQTT implementation (tracking issue wled/WLED#207) did NOT ship in 16.0.0 or 16.0.1 — the topic layout above is unchanged in current source, though the notice remains posted. The MQTT change that did land in 16.0.0 is mDNS broker discovery (.local broker hostnames are resolved via mDNS), which is additive.

mqtt_topics.description: Default device topic when none is configured; {mac} is the lowercase MAC with no separators. Payload is a brightness value 0-255, or "ON", "OFF" or "T" to toggle.
mqtt_topics.name: Device command topic

mqtt_topics.description: Colour as hex (#RRGGBB or #WWRRGGBB) or as a 32-bit decimal.
mqtt_topics.name: Device colour topic

mqtt_topics.description: Full API access over MQTT: the payload is either a /win-style query string or a JSON state object. Anything the JSON API can do can be done here, which also means broker access equals device control.
mqtt_topics.name: Device API topic

mqtt_topics.description: The XML API response — the same document /win returns.
mqtt_topics.name: Full state status

mqtt_topics.description: Physical button state, for using a controller's button as an input elsewhere.
mqtt_topics.name: Button event

mqtt_topics.description: Motion sensor state on builds wired for one.
mqtt_topics.name: Motion sensor event

realtime_protocols.description: Per-pixel streaming interfaces. All of these bypass the effect engine: the controller shows exactly the pixels it is sent, and ignores its own state until the stream stops and the timeout lapses. state.live goes true while this is happening, and state.lor decides whether a client can take control back. A client that sets a colour over the JSON API and sees nothing change should check state.live first — the usual cause is another sender still holding the device.

protocols.description: WLED's own peer-to-peer sync — how one controller mirrors its state to others. Also the channel /json/nodes is populated from.
protocols.name: WLED notifier / sync
protocols.port_source: Default; read info.udpport rather than assuming it.

protocols.description: Byte 0 = 1, byte 1 = timeout seconds, then 4-byte tuples of LED index plus RGB.
protocols.name: WARLS

protocols.description: Byte 0 = 2, byte 1 = timeout seconds, then sequential RGB triplets from index 0.
protocols.name: DRGB

protocols.description: As DRGB with a fourth white channel per pixel.
protocols.name: DRGBW

protocols.description: Byte 0 = 4, byte 1 = timeout, bytes 2-3 = start index, then sequential RGB. The start index is what lifts the 490-pixel ceiling: a sender splits a long strip across several packets.
protocols.name: DNRGB

protocols.description: White-channel variant of DNRGB. Present in current source (wled00/udp.cpp) but absent from the upstream docs table as of v16.0.1.
protocols.name: DNRGBW

protocols.description: ANSI E1.31 over multicast or unicast. Up to 9 adjacent universes, 170 LEDs (510 DMX channels) per universe. The 9-universe figure is the ESP8266 limit and the one the docs quote; current const.h allows 12 universes on ESP32 and 20 on Ethernet builds. The interoperable choice — every lighting console and xLights speaks it.
protocols.name: E1.31 (sACN)

protocols.description: Accepted since WLED 0.10.0, sharing E1.31's universe and DMX-mode configuration.
protocols.name: Art-Net

protocols.description: Distributed Display Protocol, accepted since WLED 0.11.0. 1440 channels per packet, 10-byte header. Always uses Multi RGB regardless of the configured DMX mode, so the DMX-mode setting does not apply. The efficient choice for large single-controller installs.
protocols.name: DDP

protocols.description: Accepted on its own fixed port, configured in Sync settings.
protocols.name: TPM2.net

protocols.description: Ambient-lighting protocol, protocol byte 0 on its own port.
protocols.name: Hyperion

protocols.description: Pre-processed audio data for sound-reactive builds — WLED SR and MoonModules. Not present in mainline WLED without the sound-reactive usermod, which is the practical difference between the firmware variants an app has to handle.
protocols.name: UDP sound sync (v2)

realtime_mode_values.description: REALTIME_MODE_* from wled00/const.h — the source that is driving the LEDs while state.live is true. Useful for telling a user which sender has the device rather than only that something does.

websocket.description: Push channel carrying the same state object the JSON API returns, emitted on change. This is what a responsive client should use instead of polling /json/state: WLED devices are single-core microcontrollers also driving the LED bus, and a client polling at UI framerate degrades the very animation it is displaying.
websocket.notes: The socket carries state and info in the same shape as /json/si. Sending a state object over the socket applies it, so a client need not fall back to HTTP for writes. Connection capacity is small — a couple of concurrent clients — so an app should hold one socket per device, not one per view.
